Saturday, 10 July. Dinner on Karim and Leïla’s terrace. Topic of the evening: Radu is coming to Lyon in September on Erasmus. Where should he live?
So Radu’s coming in September? Where’s he going to live?
With us, of course! I think it’s the best solution. We have a small spare room.
I don’t agree. In my opinion, he should live in the student residence, with the other students.
Exactly. I know my brother. If he lives with us, he’ll only speak Romanian with me, and he won’t meet anyone.
She’s right, Julien. When I was a student in Montréal, I learnt English thanks to my flatmates, not thanks to the classes.
On the one hand, that’s true. On the other, a residence is expensive, and he doesn’t have much money.
I don’t think that’s a real problem. Erasmus students get a grant. And residences aren’t that expensive in Lyon.
Maybe. But I don’t think he knows how to cook. He’ll eat pasta every day!
Ha! You’re wrong. My grandmother taught him to make sarmale this summer. He wrote to me yesterday.
On the other hand, he should come and eat at your place on Sundays. That’s compulsory in every family.
Right… You’ve convinced me. I think it’s a good compromise: the residence during the week, and Sundays with us.
You see? When we talk things through, we always find a solution.
And you two, don’t you think it’s time to buy a bigger flat? For… the future?
(she blushes) Leïla! That’s another debate. And tonight, I’m not giving my opinion!

Je pense que… / Je crois que…
DON’T say “Je suis d’avis que…” in an ordinary conversation (it sounds very formal), and never “Selon moi, je pense que…” (it’s repetitive).

An important rule: after “je pense que / je crois que” in the POSITIVE, the verb is in the indicative (it’s a firm opinion). In the NEGATIVE or in a question, doubt appears, so you use the SUBJUNCTIVE:
Je pense que c’est une bonne idée.
Je ne pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.
Je ne crois pas qu’il sache cuisiner.
I don’t think he knows how to cook.
Je ne trouve pas que ce soit cher.
In everyday speech, French people often use the indicative even in the negative (“Je pense pas que c’est…”), but in writing and careful French the subjunctive is required.
The French love debating at the table. Disagreeing isn’t rude if you say it with “Je comprends ton point de vue, mais…” (I understand your point of view, but…).
On the one hand it’s practical; on the other, it’s expensive.
The advantage is that he’ll meet people.
The residence is far away. On the other hand, it isn’t expensive.
In the end, I think it’s a good compromise.

On 14 July, the national holiday, the whole city of Lyon was getting ready for the fireworks. Since the morning, blue, white and red flags had been hanging from the balconies, and soldiers were parading on Place Bellecour.

In the evening, Ioana and Julien went to fetch Hélène from the care home. Madame Bernard came too, with a blanket and a flask of coffee. They settled on the Fourvière esplanade, from where you can see the whole city, the two rivers and, on a clear day, the Alps.
There were lots of people. Families with children, couples in love, groups of young people laughing loudly. Almost everyone had a phone in their hand.

“Look at them,” said Madame Bernard, shaking her head. “They don’t even look at the view. They look at their screens. In my opinion, young people today no longer know how to enjoy the present moment.”

Ioana didn’t agree. “I understand what you mean, but I don’t think it’s that simple. When I came to France, alone, my phone was my only link with my family. Thanks to it, I saw my mother every evening.”
Hélène smiled. “She’s right, Odile. In our day, when someone went far away, you waited weeks for a letter. Sometimes the letter never came.” She didn’t say Henri’s name. She didn’t need to.
Madame Bernard thought for a moment. “On the one hand, you’re both right. On the other, I still think people talk to each other less than before. On the metro, nobody says hello.”
“That’s true,” said Julien, laughing. “But in Lyon nobody has ever said hello on the metro, not even in 1960!” The two old ladies laughed, because they knew he was right.

“There was no metro in Lyon in 1960,” Hélène corrected. “It was built in 1978.” Julien raised his hands. “You see? Another argument for me: you couldn’t ignore each other on a metro that didn’t exist!”

The discussion went on, cheerful and lively, the way only the French know how to argue. They talked about France and Romania, about food (Madame Bernard thought Lyon cooking was the best in the world; Ioana didn’t think that was true, because of the sarmale), about the young, the old, love and the passing of time.
At one point, Hélène turned to Ioana. “And you, my dear, you haven’t said anything for ten minutes. Are you tired? You’re very pale.”
“A bit,” answered Ioana. “It’s work, I think. The care home project. And then… I don’t know, for a few days I haven’t felt like coffee. Even the smell bothers me. That’s strange, isn’t it?”

Hélène and Madame Bernard looked at each other. For a second, there was exactly the same light in their eyes. Madame Bernard, who had been a doctor for forty years, opened her mouth to say something. Hélène put her hand gently on her arm. Madame Bernard closed her mouth again.
“I don’t think it’s anything serious,” said Hélène with a mysterious smile. “But in your place, I’d go and see a doctor next week. Just to be sure.”

At that moment, the first rocket exploded above the Saône. Red, then green, then gold. The whole esplanade cried “Oh!” at the same time. The young people raised their phones to film. Madame Bernard sighed, then she took hers out too.

“It’s for Isabelle,” she explained, a little embarrassed. “She’s in Paris, she can’t see the Lyon fireworks.” Ioana laughed. “You see? Phones aren’t so bad.” Madame Bernard shrugged. “I never said I was right. I only said it was my opinion.”
The fireworks lasted twenty minutes. Julien was holding Ioana’s hand. Hélène was holding Madame Bernard’s hand. And below them, the whole city was shining, like a great illuminated piano.
After taking Hélène back, Ioana and Julien walked down the steps of the hill. It was past midnight. The streets smelt of gunpowder and summer. Groups of young people were still singing on the quays.

“You know,” said Julien, “I think Madame Bernard isn’t completely wrong. We look at our screens too much. Tonight, during the fireworks, I decided not to film. I just wanted to watch them with you.” Ioana squeezed his hand. “Me too. But I don’t think it’s a question of age. It’s a question of choice.”

On the bridge, Ioana’s phone buzzed. It was Radu, who never went to bed before two in the morning. “Good news! I’ve got a room in the residence, near the university. But don’t worry: I’ll come and eat at your place every Sunday. And every Wednesday. And maybe Fridays too.”

That night Ioana couldn’t sleep. She kept thinking about the look Hélène and Madame Bernard had exchanged on the esplanade. It wasn’t a worried look. It was something else. A kind of secret joy, as if they knew something she didn’t know yet.

She looked at Julien, asleep next to her with his mouth open, like a child. Then she counted on her fingers, in the dark. Once. Twice. She sat up in bed, her heart pounding. “No…” she whispered. “It’s not possible. Or… is it?”
The next morning, before going to work, she stopped at the chemist’s in Croix-Rousse. The one that used to be Lucette’s café. She thought it was a sign. But that’s another story.
